title: Is One Tree Part of Another
statement: Given two binary trees `root` and `sub`, return `true` if `sub` appears **as a subtree** of `root`: there is a node in `root` such that the tree that starts at that node (the node and **all** of its descendants) has exactly the **same shape and the same values** as `sub`. The empty tree is a subtree of every tree (including the empty one); a non-empty `sub` is never a subtree of an empty `root`.
constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in each tree <= 2000

examples.explanation: The node 3 with its children 6 and 7 is exactly `sub`.
The node 3 has the extra child 7, so its subtree is not equal to [3, 6].

expected.time: O(n * m) simple, O(n + m) with serialisation

hints.nudge: First solve a smaller problem: are two trees exactly equal? Then ask where in the big tree you should compare.
hints.pattern: Compare `sub` with the subtree at EVERY node of `root` using a same-tree check; or write both trees as texts (preorder with markers for missing children) and test whether one text contains the other.
hints.pseudocode:
same(a, b): both missing -> true; one missing -> false; a.val == b.val and same(a.left, b.left) and same(a.right, b.right)
isSubtree(root, sub): if sub is missing: true; if root is missing: false; same(root, sub) or isSubtree(root.left, sub) or isSubtree(root.right, sub)
hints.walkthrough: A subtree must match completely down to the leaves: a node and ALL its descendants. So at each node of `root` run an equality check against `sub` (compare values, then both children recursively, treating a missing child as different from a present one). That costs up to O(n * m). To make it linear, serialise each tree in preorder and write a marker for every missing child, for example `^3,^4,#,#,^5,#,#`: this text identifies the shape and the values uniquely. Put a comma and the `^` in front of each value so that 12 cannot match inside 112. `sub` is a subtree exactly when its text occurs inside the text of `root`, and a substring search is O(n + m) with a good algorithm.
